questions.q: Why is cost, latency, and quality described as a three-way trade-off rather than three independent knobs?
options: Because the three are completely unrelated to each other
Because in almost every serving decision, improving two of them usually comes at the expense of the third
Because only one of the three can ever be changed at a time
Because quality cannot be measured, so it isn't part of the trade-off
questions.explain: A bigger model raises quality but costs more and adds latency; a smaller/quantized model lowers cost and latency but risks quality; more replicas lower latency but raise cost. Rarely can all three improve simultaneously.

questions.q: Why are the Chapter 4 techniques (KV cache, paged attention, continuous batching) described as mostly 'free wins'?
options: They are literally free of charge from cloud providers
They improve throughput and latency by computing the same result more efficiently, rather than approximating or reducing quality
They eliminate the need for any GPU hardware
They always reduce model quality in exchange for lower cost
questions.explain: These techniques make the exact same computation more efficient (less wasted memory, more efficient batching) rather than trading away accuracy, so they raise throughput/lower latency without a quality cost.

questions.q: According to the recommended practical order of operations, what should be set first?
options: The lowest possible cost, regardless of other requirements
The quality floor and latency ceiling, based on actual user or business requirements
The exact GPU vendor to use
The marketing copy for the product
questions.explain: The suggested order sets the quality floor and latency ceiling from real requirements first, applies free wins next, and only then minimizes cost within what's left — rather than optimizing cost first and backfilling the rest.

questions.q: What risk does optimizing cost first, before setting quality and latency requirements, create?
options: It guarantees the best possible outcome on all three dimensions
It can quietly erode quality or latency until someone notices, since cost-cutting isn't bounded by any floor or ceiling
It has no risk at all
It always improves quality as a side effect
questions.explain: Without a quality floor or latency ceiling set in advance, pure cost optimization has nothing stopping it from degrading the other two dimensions until the product has quietly gotten worse.

questions.q: Where do Chapter 3's techniques (quantization, pruning, distillation) land on the cost/latency/quality triangle?
options: They have no effect on any of the three dimensions
They move along the cost/latency vs. quality axis — lowering cost and latency with a quality cost that must be measured, not assumed
They always improve quality while increasing cost
They only affect network latency, never compute cost
questions.explain: Quantization, pruning, and distillation trade some model quality for lower cost and latency. The actual quality impact needs to be measured (as Chapter 3 covered), not assumed to be negligible.
